texts.title: Wait for It
texts.subtitle: In an age of unlimited free photos, a growing number of teenagers are paying for 36 pictures and a week’s wait. Why?
texts.sourceNote: Original text written for this mock paper.

paragraphs.text: On a Saturday afternoon in Tseung Kwan O, sixteen-year-old Chloe Tsang stands on a footbridge, holding her breath. She has one frame left on a HK$190 roll of colour film, and the sun is already touching the hills. She presses the shutter, winds the film on with her thumb and grins. “That’s it, the roll’s done – now I just wait and see if any of them came out,” she says. For a generation raised on camera phones, the delay has unexpectedly become part of the appeal.

Chloe is part of a striking consumer phenomenon. Across Hong Kong, processing shops that were preparing to close a decade ago now report weekend queues of students, while second-hand analogue cameras that once sold for a few hundred dollars change hands for several thousand. Internationally, the revival is more pronounced still: Fujifilm’s Instax instant cameras sold so poorly in the mid-2000s that the company reportedly considered discontinuing them, yet by 2016 it was selling more of them annually than its digital cameras. Most of these buyers, analysts note, are under twenty-five.

Raymond Kwok has operated a small processing laboratory in Sheung Wan since 1989, and his routine has scarcely changed. A customer drops off an exposed roll; in a darkened room, the film is fed through a sequence of chemical baths – a developer that reveals the hidden image, a bleach, and a fixer that makes the image permanent. What has changed is the final step. “In the old days everybody wanted prints, but now nine out of ten kids just want the scans emailed,” he says. “They pay for film, then look at it on a phone. I don’t get it, but business is business.”

The hobby is far from cheap. A roll of 36 colour exposures typically costs HK$150 to HK$220 in Hong Kong, and by some estimates global film prices have roughly tripled since 2016, as manufacturers struggle to satisfy demand using factories designed for a shrinking market. Developing and scanning add a further HK$70 to HK$100, so each picture costs between six and nine dollars. Instant film is no cheaper: an Instax print costs roughly HK$7, and a single Polaroid print can cost three times as much.

Veterans may find this puzzling. In 2008 Polaroid announced that it would cease manufacturing instant film, and its last factory, in Enschede in the Netherlands, closed that summer. A small group of enthusiasts and former employees bought the machinery and spent nearly two years reinventing the film, because many of the original chemicals were no longer being manufactured. Their first films were notoriously unreliable, their colours shifting and fading within months. Yet they sold – evidence, analysts argue, that some consumers will tolerate imperfection and even pay a premium for it.

Dr Helen Mak, who lectures in visual culture at a Hong Kong university, believes imperfection is precisely the point. “A digital image is endlessly correctable: you take forty versions, select one, filter it, retouch it,” she says. “Analogue introduces scarcity and delay, and those constraints change behaviour. You compose deliberately because every exposure has a cost. And you can’t curate your face before anyone sees it, because, well, you haven’t seen it either.” The grain and light leaks of inexpensive film, she argues, function as evidence of authenticity.

For Chloe, the appeal is simpler. “On my phone I’ve got, like, eleven thousand photos and I never look at them, but my film ones – maybe two hundred – I know every single one,” she says. Her favourite is badly out of focus: her grandmother laughing at a dim sum table, half her face lost in steam. “It’s a terrible photo,” she admits, “but it’s the only one where she looks like herself.”

The revival contains an obvious irony. Many teenagers who claim to have turned to film to escape the pressures of social media subsequently post their scans on social media, and some apps now sell digital filters that imitate the aesthetic of 1990s film – grain, scratches, orange date stamps – allowing a phone picture to pass as analogue. Jason Ho, 23, who sells refurbished cameras online from his flat in Kwun Tong, has no complaints. “Honestly? Half my customers found me because a film photo went viral,” he says. “Instagram is my best salesman.”

Jason’s flat is a small museum of the late twentieth century: shelves of vintage compact cameras, boxes of lenses, a drawer of tiny screws. Each camera is cleaned, tested and repaired before being listed. The most sought-after models are not expensive professional bodies but cheap “point-and-shoot” cameras that families once bought at airports. Prices have climbed so steeply that Jason worries the bubble will burst. “One day the fashion moves on,” he says, “and I’m sitting here with four hundred cameras and no buyers.”

Not every parent is delighted. Chloe’s mother, Mrs Tsang, shot rolls of film on family holidays in the 1990s and still remembers collecting packets of prints only to find half of them ruined. “We switched to digital because it was better – cheaper, easier, no waste,” she says. “Now she spends her pocket money on something I was glad to get rid of.” Environmentalists also object to the hazardous chemical waste that colour processing generates; laboratories must pay licensed collectors to remove it, an expense that, Mr Kwok grumbles, keeps rising.

Paradoxically, scarcity may be what keeps film attractive. For decades film was simply what everybody used. Today, a single tangible print cannot be copied, shared or deleted with a tap, which gives it a weight that digital images lack. One 2013 American study found that museum visitors remembered fewer details of objects they had photographed than of objects they had merely observed, as if the camera had done the remembering. Whether film photographers remember more is unproven, but many of them believe it. “With thirty-six shots,” Chloe says, “I actually look at things first.”

Analysts disagree about how long the revival can last. Manufacturers remain cautious: a new film production line costs many millions of dollars and takes years to build, and nobody wants to relive the early 2000s, when demand collapsed almost overnight. Others argue that film has found a stable niche, as vinyl records have, settling into a small but loyal market. Mr Kwok is not betting either way. “I’ve seen film die once already,” he says. “If it dies again, I’ll retire; if not, I’ll be here.”

Schools are catching the habit too. At Chloe’s school, a film photography club founded last September with six members now has thirty-one. Members share one changing bag – a light-proof sack for handling film without a darkroom – and take turns borrowing two donated cameras. Their teacher adviser, Mr Yeung, has noticed an unexpected benefit. “They argue about composition and light for half an hour before taking one picture,” he says. “I’ve been trying to make them think that hard in Visual Arts for years.”

On a Thursday evening, as Mr Kwok is pulling down his shutter, a schoolboy arrives breathless with three rolls of film. Mr Kwok labels an envelope and asks, out of habit, whether he wants prints. The boy hesitates, glances at his phone and puts it away. “Maybe just one set,” he says, “for my mum.”

texts.title: Swimmers turned away as lifeguard shortage bites
texts.sourceNote: Original text written for this mock paper.

paragraphs.text: Thousands of swimmers hoping to escape the summer heat have been turned away from public pools this month, as a shortage of lifeguards forces at least 14 pool complexes to suspend some of their services. With temperatures reaching 34°C on several days, queues formed outside some pools before 6:30am, only for swimmers to discover that the facilities they wanted were shut.

Hong Kong has around 45 public swimming pool complexes, and each pool must have a minimum number of lifeguards on duty to ensure adequate supervision before it can open. Lifeguards must hold a recognised pool lifeguard award and a first-aid certificate, and many are hired on short seasonal contracts that end when outdoor pools close in the autumn, which makes recruitment a constant struggle. According to the Pool Safety Staff Union, a group representing lifeguards, about one in five lifeguard posts was vacant at the start of the summer.

The impact varies considerably across the territory. At Pak Shek, in the New Territories, the teaching pool now opens only in the mornings. In Kowloon, one large complex has closed its diving pool for the whole summer, while a pool on Hong Kong Island has had to shut completely on four afternoons this month when lifeguards called in sick. Smaller pools on the outlying islands, which rely heavily on part-time staff, have been hit hardest of all.

Union chairman Tony Mok said the shortage was “entirely predictable”. “Every year we warn them, and every year they act surprised,” he said. “You’re asking young people to sit in the scorching sun all day, staying vigilant while hundreds of people swim, on a contract that ends in October. Then they wonder why everyone leaves to become a fitness trainer.”

A government spokesperson said that recruitment was continuing and that pay for seasonal lifeguards had been raised this year. The government has also tested a computer system that uses underwater cameras to detect swimmers in difficulty and alert personnel, but stressed that the technology was intended to assist lifeguards, not replace them. A small number of pools have also started hiring lifeguards through private companies on a trial basis.

For swimmers, the explanations offer little comfort. Retired teacher Leung Wai-man, 67, has swum at the same pool every morning for twenty years. “My doctor told me to swim for my back. Now I come here and half the pool is closed,” he said. Parents have also complained that children’s swimming classes were cancelled at short notice, and some competitive swimmers say they have been forced to train in crowded lanes alongside casual users.

Mr Mok believes the problem will return next summer unless lifeguards are offered longer contracts. “Make it a proper career and people will stay,” he said. “Make it a summer job and you’ll get summer staff.”

texts.title: Let teenagers earn their whistle
texts.subtitle: Letter to the Editor, 24 July
texts.sourceNote: Original text written for this mock paper.

paragraphs.text: Dear Editor, I read with interest your report on the lifeguard shortage (21 July). As the mother of two keen swimmers – and someone who spent three summers as a beach lifeguard in Sai Kung in the 1990s – I would like to offer a suggestion that does not seem to have occurred to anybody.

Every summer my children’s swimming classes are cancelled, and every summer I am told that there is “nothing we can do”. Frankly, I am tired of hearing it. Hong Kong has thousands of strong teenage swimmers who spend July and August staring at their phones. Many of them would jump at the chance to earn some money doing something useful outdoors – if only someone would show them how.

When I was sixteen, my school ran a lifesaving club. Twice a week, after lessons, a retired lifeguard put us through our paces in the school pool: towing each other across the deep end, eyes stinging from the chlorine, diving for a rubber brick, practising resuscitation on a plastic dummy we nicknamed Uncle Ming. By the time we left school, half of us had our first awards. The club was a lifeline for the public pool next door, which recruited several of us every summer.

My proposal is simple. First, the government should fund lifesaving clubs in secondary schools that have their own pools, and allow schools without pools to share facilities. Second, pools should be encouraged to take on trained sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds for part-time shifts alongside experienced staff. Third, students who complete their awards should receive a small allowance, so that families who cannot afford the course fees are not left out.

Some will say that teenagers are too young for such responsibility. I disagree. A well-trained seventeen-year-old working under proper supervision is far safer than an empty lifeguard chair. In many countries, it is perfectly normal for students to work as pool lifeguards during the holidays, and many of them carry on long after they have left school.
The shortage will not be solved by apologising for it every July. If we train them young, we may find that some of them stay for much longer than a summer. Yours faithfully, Grace Fung, Ma On Shan

texts.title: The Thumb Trap
texts.subtitle: Our apps are built to be hard to put down. Is that a scandal, or simply good business?
texts.sourceNote: Original text written for this mock paper.

paragraphs.text: I began writing this essay at nine o’clock this morning. By eleven I had produced two sentences and watched a stranger restore a rusty kitchen knife, all because I had picked up my phone to look up a single word and the phone, as it so often does, had other ideas.

I mention this not as a confession but as evidence. For years I blamed my vanishing mornings on my own feeble willpower, a comfortable explanation precisely because it made the problem small and private, and one I now consider largely mistaken. The apps on my phone are not neutral tools that I happen to misuse; many have been meticulously engineered, by some of the best-paid graduates of my generation, to do exactly what they did to me this morning.

The underlying idea predates the smartphone. In 1971 the economist Herbert Simon observed that “a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention”, and half a century later his insight has become a business model. Most apps are free because we are not really their customers; the customers are advertisers, and what they purchase is our attention – measured in minutes, auctioned by the second and harvested as efficiently as a crop of wheat.

Consider the infinite scroll. Until the mid-2000s web pages ended, and a reader who wanted more had to click “next”, a tiny moment of decision in which she might equally decide to stop. Infinite scroll, devised in 2006 to make browsing smoother, eliminated that moment by refilling the page automatically as the reader approaches the end. Autoplay, which starts the next video before you have chosen it, performs the same service for television.

Then there are notifications, the red badges and buzzes that interrupt us dozens of times a day. Many are strictly unnecessary – a friend of a friend is “live” – but each is a small invitation to return, because engagement, as the industry calls it, is monitored hour by hour, and an app that loses it soon loses its commercial value.

The most powerful mechanism, however, is borrowed from the casino. In the 1950s the psychologist B. F. Skinner found that pigeons pecked most persistently at a disc when food arrived unpredictably, sometimes after two pecks and sometimes after fifty. Slot machines exploit this principle, and so, critics argue, does the “pull-to-refresh” gesture: you drag your thumb down, wait, and something new appears – or doesn’t. Every refresh is a small gamble, and like most gamblers, we remember the wins.

I put some of this to a former product designer, whom I shall call Ben because he still works in the industry and would like to keep it that way. “Nobody sat in a meeting and said, ‘Let’s make people addicted,’” he told me. “We said, ‘Let’s increase daily active users by three per cent.’ But if you chase that number long enough, you end up in the same place.”

What troubled him most was how trivial each decision had seemed: a button moved slightly lower on the screen, a half-second delay inserted before a new “like” appeared so that it arrived like a surprise. Every change was tested on millions of users, and the version that kept people scrolling longest invariably won. “You never see a face,” he said. “You see a graph going up, and it’s very easy to feel proud of a graph.”

The costs are harder to quantify than the profits. Surveys regularly find that many teenagers in the United States believe they spend too much time on their phones, and some researchers associate heavy social media use with poorer sleep and lower mood. Others are unconvinced: one widely discussed 2019 analysis of data from more than 350,000 adolescents concluded that the link between technology use and wellbeing was real but tiny, roughly as strong as the link with eating potatoes.

This is a fair point, and I have no wish to join the queue of people shouting at new technology. Yet the potato comparison tells us only that the average effect is modest; it says nothing about whether apps are designed to hold us for longer than we would freely choose. Nobody has ever employed a team of engineers to make a boiled potato harder to stop eating.

The industry’s defenders usually reach for one of four arguments. Users, they say, are adults who can decide independently how to spend their time; every business, from supermarkets to novelists who end chapters on cliffhangers, tries to hold its customers’ interest; the services are free and genuinely valuable; and the companies already provide tools, such as screen-time limits, for anyone who wishes to cut down.

The first argument is the one I find hardest to accept. Of course we choose to pick up our phones, but a choice made against an opponent who has studied you and learnt exactly when you are tired, lonely or bored is not quite a free choice. It is rather like playing chess against someone who can see which piece you are about to move: you are still playing, but you are unlikely to win.

Professor Ruth Abara, a behavioural economist, is blunter. “We talk about attention spans shrinking as if it were a natural process, like coastal erosion,” she told me. “It isn’t. Our attention hasn’t been worn away by the weather. It’s been mined, deliberately, by companies with shareholders.”

Abara has little faith in willpower as a solution. “Telling individuals to resist this is like telling someone to stay dry by walking faster in the rain,” she says. “You need an umbrella, and umbrellas are made by somebody else.” The umbrellas she has in mind are regulations: limits on autoplay for children, restrictions on endless feeds for under-sixteens and a requirement that apps offer an honest stopping point, measures several governments are cautiously considering.

I agree with her, with one reservation: regulations tend to arrive a decade after the problem they address. In the meantime, I have acquired my own small umbrella, an inexpensive alarm clock that allows my phone to spend the night in the kitchen. It is a minor gesture, and it has not cured me, but it has given me back the first twenty minutes of every day, which is more than any app has ever offered to return.

I finished this essay at four in the afternoon. My phone informs me, with characteristic precision, that I picked it up 71 times in the process, a figure I have decided to regard as exaggerated – which is, I suspect, exactly what the app would like me to do.

paragraphs.text: DevInDublin · 2 days ago: App developer here. “Ben” is right, but the writer skips the boring part: most of us would love to make calmer products. Calm doesn’t pay for the servers. Fix the business model and the design will fix itself.

mira_k · 1 day ago: Ban endless feeds for under-16s? I’m fifteen. I’d just use my mum’s account. Teach us how this stuff works instead – learning about the slot machine thing actually made me use my phone less.

S. Okafor · 20 hours ago: The potato study keeps being misused by both sides. A small average effect can hide a large effect on a minority of very heavy users, and that is where researchers should look next.
